en: Thus have I heard: The Samaṇamuṇḍika Sutta (Discourse to Samaṇa Muṇḍika), Majjhima Nikāya 78. Thus have I heard: [One time the Blessed One was staying at... [text continues]... Thus have I heard.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the wanderer Uggāhamāna Samaṇamuṇḍikāputta was residing in Mallikā’s Park,
a single-hall *tinduka*-grove used for debating doctrines, together with a large assembly of wanderers.
[Accompanied] by about five hundred wanderers.
Then the carpenter Pañcakaṅga departed from Sāvatthī in the middle of the day to see the Blessed One.
Then this thought occurred to the carpenter Pañcakaṅga:
“It is not yet the time to see the Blessed One;
the Blessed One is in seclusion.
It is also not the right time to see the monks who are worthy of veneration.”
"The monks are in seclusion, developing their minds.
What if I were to go to the park of Mallikā—the Samayappavādaka, Tindukācīra, Ekasālaka—to where the wanderer Uggāhamāna, the son of Samaṇa Muṇḍikā, is staying?
Then the carpenter Pañcakaṅga went to the park of Mallikā—the Samayappavādaka, Tindukācīra, Ekasālaka—to where the wanderer Uggāhamāna, the son of Samaṇa Muṇḍikā, was staying.
Now at that time, the wanderer Uggāhamāna Sāmaṇamuṇḍikāputta was seated together with a large assembly of wanderers who were making a great clamor and loud noise,
engaged in various kinds of frivolous talk, such as:
Talk about kings, talk about thieves, talk about ministers, talk about armies, talk about dangers, talk about battles, talk about food, talk about drinks,
talk about clothing, talk about bedding, talk about garlands, talk about scents, talk about relatives,
talk about vehicles, talk about villages, talk about towns, talk about cities, talk about districts, talk about women, talk about heroes, and talk about streets.
...talk about pots, talk about departed relatives, talk on diversity, talk about the origin of the world, talk about the origin of the ocean, or talk about "thus it was" and "thus it will be.
Then the wanderer Uggāhamāna, son of Muṇḍikā, saw the carpenter Pañcakanga coming from afar.
Seeing him, he quieted his own assembly:
“Be quiet, sirs; do not make a noise.
This is the householder Pañcakanga, the carpenter, who is a disciple of the ascetic Gotama.
Indeed, he is one among those white-robed lay disciples of the ascetic Gotama who reside here in Sāvatthī.”
“Those venerable ones desire little noise, are disciplined in regard to little noise, and speak in praise of little noise;
perhaps, having perceived an assembly with little noise, they might think it fit to approach.
Then those wanderers became silent.
Then the carpenter Pañcakanga approached the wanderer Uggāhamāna, the son of Samaṇamuṇḍikā; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the wanderer Uggāhamāna, the son of Samaṇamuṇḍikā.
After exchanging polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. As the carpenter Pañcakanga was sitting there, the wanderer Uggāhamāna, the son of Samaṇamuṇḍikā, said this to him:
“Householder, I describe a person endowed with four qualities as one who has perfected what is wholesome, who is supremely wholesome, who has attained the highest goal, an unshakable ascetic.
With which four?
Here, householder, one does not commit evil deeds by way of body, does not speak evil speech, does not entertain evil intentions, and does not live by an evil livelihood.”

“Householder, it is on account of these four qualities that I describe a person as a perfected ascetic—one accomplished in virtue, supremely virtuous, who has attained the highest goal, and is unshakable.
Then the carpenter Pañcakanga neither approved nor rejected the words of the wanderer Uggāhamāna Samaṇamuṇḍikāputta.
Without approving or rejecting them, he rose from his seat and departed.
“I shall understand the meaning of these words in the presence of the Blessed One.
Then the carpenter Pañcakanga approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Sitting there, the carpenter Pañcakanga reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation and dialogue that had taken place with the wanderer Uggāhamāna, the son of Samaṇamuṇḍikā.
When this was said, the Blessed One said to the carpenter Pañcakaṅga:
“If that were so, carpenter, then a young boy, tender and lying on his back, would become more accomplished, more supremely skilled,
and have attained the highest goal than the ascetic Ayojjha, just as [the case of] the wanderer Uggāhamāna.”
This is the word of Samaṇa Muṇḍikāputta.
For a young, tender infant lying on its back, householder, there is not even what is called a "body," so how could it perform an evil deed with the body, other than mere movement?
For a young, tender infant lying on its back, householder, there is not even what is called "speech," so how could it utter evil speech, other than mere crying?
"For a young child, householder, who is weak and lies on his back, even the thought of volition does not exist; how much less will he form an evil thought, other than mere crying?
For a young child, householder, who is weak and lies on his back, even the means of livelihood does not exist; how much less will he live by an evil livelihood, other than mother's milk?
This being so, householder, a young child who is weak and lies on his back would be accomplished in what is wholesome."
The ascetic Ayojjha is supremely skilled and has attained the highest goal, according to the words of the wanderer Uggāhamāna Samaṇamuṇḍikāputta.
However, carpenter, I do not describe a person as such even when they possess four qualities...
He does not approach a recluse who is accomplished in wholesome qualities, supremely wholesome, and who has attained the highest goal;
rather, he stands having seized this young boy, who is tender and still lying on his back.
By what four [qualities]?
"Here, carpenter, one does not commit evil deeds by way of body, does not utter evil speech, does not entertain evil intentions,
and does not live by an evil livelihood. It is on account of these four qualities, carpenter, that I describe a person as neither accomplished in what is wholesome,
nor supreme in what is wholesome, nor having attained the highest goal, nor an unshakable ascetic."
He stands having seized this young boy, tender and lying on his back.
But, carpenter, it is one endowed with ten qualities whom I describe as a person perfected in skill, supremely skilled, who has attained the highest goal, an unshakable ascetic.
These are unwholesome virtues.
"I say, carpenter, that this must be understood.
Unwholesome qualities originate from this;
I say, carpenter, that this must be understood."
"Here, unwholesome habits cease without remainder;
that, carpenter, I say should be understood.
One who practices in this way is practicing for the cessation of unwholesome habits."
"I say, master carpenter, that this should be understood.
These are wholesome virtues;
I say, master carpenter, that this should be understood."
Virtues originating from desire are wholesome;
I say, carpenter, that this must be understood.
Here, wholesome virtues cease without remainder.
"That, carpenter, I say should be understood.
One who practices in such a way is practicing for the cessation of wholesome virtues;
that, carpenter, I say should be understood."
"These are unwholesome intentions;
that, carpenter, I say should be understood.
Unwholesome intentions originate from this."
"I say, master carpenter, that this must be understood.
Here, unwholesome intentions cease without remainder;
I say, master carpenter, that this must be understood."
One who practices in this way is practicing for the cessation of unwholesome intentions.
"This, master carpenter, is what I say should be understood:
these are wholesome intentions."
"I say, master carpenter, that this must be understood.
Wholesome intentions originate from this;
I say, master carpenter, that this must be understood."
"Here, carpenter, wholesome intentions cease without remainder;
that, I say, should be understood.
One who practices in this way is practicing for the cessation of wholesome intentions."
"That, carpenter, I say, should be understood.
And what, carpenter, are unwholesome virtues?
Unwholesome bodily action, unwholesome verbal action, and a wrong livelihood."
"These, carpenter, are called unwholesome virtues.
And what, carpenter, is the origin of these unwholesome virtues?
Their origin has also been stated."
“It should be said: ‘arisen from consciousness.
What is consciousness?
For consciousness is manifold, of many kinds, and of various types.”
Whatever mind is accompanied by lust, accompanied by hatred, and accompanied by delusion—from this, unwholesome virtues arise.
And where, carpenter, do these unwholesome virtues cease without remainder?
Their cessation has also been taught.
Here, carpenter, a bhikkhu abandons bodily misconduct and develops bodily good conduct;
he abandons verbal misconduct and develops verbal good conduct; he abandons mental misconduct and develops mental good conduct;
and abandoning wrong livelihood, he maintains his life by right livelihood.
It is here that these unwholesome habits cease without remainder.
How, master builder, does one practice for the cessation of unwholesome habits?
Here, master builder, a bhikkhu generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the non-arising of evil, unwholesome states that have not yet arisen.
He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the abandoning of evil, unwholesome states that have arisen;
he generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen;

he generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the stability, non-confusion, increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of wholesome states that have arisen.
"Practicing in this way, carpenter, one is practicing for the cessation of unwholesome virtues.
And what, carpenter, are wholesome virtues?
Wholesome bodily action, wholesome verbal action, and I also say, carpenter, that purity of livelihood is virtue."
"These, carpenter, are called wholesome virtues.
And what, carpenter, is the origin of these wholesome virtues?
Their origin has also been stated."
"It should be said: 'arisen from consciousness.
What is consciousness?
For consciousness is indeed manifold, of many kinds, and of various types."
Whatever mind is free from lust, free from hatred, and free from delusion—whence do the wholesome virtues originate?
And where, carpenter, do these wholesome virtues cease without remainder?
Their cessation has also been taught.
"In this case, carpenter, a bhikkhu is virtuous but does not identify with his virtue;
he understands, as it really is, that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those wholesome virtues of his cease without remainder.
And how, carpenter, is one practicing for the cessation of wholesome virtues?"

“Here, carpenter, a bhikkhu generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts the mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil unwholesome states; he generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts the mind, and strives for the abandoning of arisen evil unwholesome states; [and] he generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts the mind, and strives for the arising of unarisen wholesome states.”...
[as above] ... “...for the maintenance, stability, increase, development, and perfection of arisen wholesome states.”... [as above] ...

He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the stability, non-confusion, increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of wholesome states that have arisen.
One who practices in this way, carpenter, is practicing for the cessation of wholesome virtues.
And what, carpenter, are unwholesome intentions?
Sensual intention, ill will intention, and cruelty intention—
these, master builder, are called unwholesome intentions.
And what, master builder, is the origin of these unwholesome intentions?
Their origination has also been stated.
It should be said: "They originate from perception.
What is perception?
For perceptions are indeed many, of various kinds, and of diverse types:
perception of sensual desire, perception of ill will, and perception of cruelty—
these are unwholesome intentions originating from this [mind].
"And where, master carpenter, do these unwholesome intentions cease without remainder?
Their cessation has also been taught.
Here, master carpenter, quite secluded from sensual pleasures... [a bhikkhu] enters and dwells in the first jhāna."
It is here that these unwholesome intentions cease without remainder.
And how, master builder, does one practice for the cessation of unwholesome intentions?
Here, master builder, a bhikkhu generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the non-arising of evil, unwholesome states that have not yet arisen.

He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states; ... for the arising of unarisen wholesome states; ... and for the stability, non-confusion, increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of arisen wholesome states.
"Practicing in this way, carpenter, one is practicing for the cessation of unwholesome intentions.
And what, carpenter, are wholesome intentions?
The intention of renunciation, the intention of non-ill will, and the intention of non-cruelty."
"These, carpenter, are called wholesome intentions.
And what, carpenter, is the origin of these wholesome intentions?
Their origin has also been stated."
‘Arising from perception’ is what should be said.
What is perception?
For perception is also many, of various kinds, and of diverse types.
The perception of renunciation, the perception of non-ill will, and the perception of non-cruelty—
from these arise wholesome intentions. And where, master builder, do these wholesome intentions cease without remainder?
Their cessation has also been stated.
Here, master carpenter, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna;
herein these wholesome intentions cease without remainder.
And how, master carpenter, is one practicing for the cessation of wholesome intentions?

Here, master carpenter, a bhikkhu generates desire, exerts effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states; [he generates desire, exerts effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives] for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states... [as before].

He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the arising of unarisen wholesome states... [and so on] ...for the stability, non-confusion, increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of arisen wholesome states.
It is by practicing in this way, carpenter, that one is practicing for the cessation of wholesome intentions.
"And by what ten qualities, master builder, do I describe a person as endowed with skill, supremely skilled, having attained the highest attainment, an unshakable ascetic?
Here, master builder, a bhikkhu is endowed with the right view of one beyond training; he is endowed with the right intention of one beyond training;
he is endowed with the right speech of one beyond training; he is endowed with the right action of one beyond training."
He is endowed with right livelihood of one beyond training; he is endowed with right effort of one beyond training;
he is endowed with right mindfulness of one beyond training; he is endowed with right concentration of one beyond training;
he is endowed with right knowledge of one beyond training; he is endowed with right liberation of one beyond training.
“Indeed, carpenter, it is one who possesses these ten qualities that I describe as a person accomplished in skill, supremely skilled, who has attained the highest goal, an unshakable ascetic.
This is what the Blessed One said.
Delighted, the carpenter Pañcakanga rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Samaṇamuṇḍika Sutta, the eighth, is finished.
